Your Name on the Door.name: Your Name on the Door
Your Name on the Door.description:
🏢 A brand-new agency opens its door: one desk, one sidekick, a dispatch radio and rent due Friday.

📍 Hero Agency Row, Musutafu · Monday morning
🎭 Busy, proud, a little broke
👥 For Licensed Pro Heroes
Your Name on the Door.storyStart:
THE SITUATION: It is a crisp Monday morning in Musutafu, the first day of classes at U.A. Academy. You are a licensed pro hero who has just opened an agency of your own on Hero Agency Row, the converted office block where several small agencies share a garage and compete for every call. Your agency has one office, one eager sidekick on a first-month contract, a part-time office manager, and a lease paid through Friday. Your Hero Public Safety Commission registration came through last week, and your agency's name is fresh on the Billboard Chart's bottom pages. Since the news broke that All Might teaches at U.A., the whole city is watching heroes.

THE PLACE: Hero Agency Row: your second-floor office behind a frosted-glass door where your agency's logo still smells of fresh paint. Inside sit a front desk, two work desks, a humming dispatch radio, morning light across the floor, and a wall map of Musutafu with no pins yet. Down the hall, the rival agencies' doors stay shut; downstairs lie the shared ready room and the echoing patrol garage.

THE MOMENT: Your office manager is reading out the week's bills over the smell of fresh coffee when the dispatch radio crackles: a stray Quirk fight has broken out near Musutafu Station, no agency is on scene yet, and the agency down the hall is already pulling its van out of the garage.

WHO MAY APPEAR:
- Death Arms and Backdraft: share the downstairs garage; Death Arms barks orders, Backdraft counts heads.
- Gunhead and Fourth Kind: neighbors on the Row; Gunhead is kind and soft-spoken, Fourth Kind is gruff and terse.
- Kamui Woods and Mount Lady: rising Musutafu pros who fiercely compete for the same front-page headlines.
- Sansa Tamakawa: the cat-headed police officer who takes statements; courteous and exact.
- Naomasa Tsukauchi: the veteran detective, if a case touches the League of Villains.

OPENING HOOKS:
- Licensed Pro Hero: the very first call of your agency's life, a rival van already rolling out, and your sidekick waiting on your orders.
- Hero Family: a famous parent's loud congratulations arrive as a towering flower stand in the hallway that the whole Row cannot miss.
- Wealthy Family: the week's lease was paid by family money, and an opinionated relative already has notes about your logo.
- Criminal Ties: a familiar face from the dim alley bars walks right in asking to hire a licensed hero, cash in hand.
- default: the crackling radio, the stack of bills, and the empty wall map, all demanding you at once.

THE AGENCY'S PEOPLE: your sidekick and your office manager are your own staff: ordinary people the narration names with ordinary Japanese names the first time it shows them, and they keep those names. Each took this job for a reason of their own, has real opinions about the agency, and says them; the sidekick follows lawful orders, asks about unclear ones, and refuses unlawful ones. Neither is a canon character. The brisk voice on the dispatch radio is a dispatcher, quoted in narration with a name. Your office manager runs the phone, the appointments, and the bills, and knows which one can wait. The sidekick's first-month contract pays at the end of the month: late pay costs trust, and an unpaid sidekick can quit.

THE FIRST DAYS: an agency owner's week runs to routine: a morning briefing with your sidekick, patrols of the contracted streets, calls from dispatch, a report after every capture, police statements, the Commission's incident app, meetings with sponsors or the landlord, an evening patrol, and the bills. On the Row, the Ready Room holds the lockers and the shared patrol whiteboard, and the Patrol Garage smells of oil and holds the shared bikes, two small vans, and the repair bench.

HOW CALLS AND MONEY WORK: dispatch announces an incident on the shared band; any agency may respond; the capture belongs to whoever restrains the suspect, and the police take custody. Pay follows resolved incidents and contracts; sponsors pay for visibility; property damage is billed to the agency. Friday's rent is a real deadline: you can pay it, earn it, borrow it, or negotiate it, and missing it brings the landlord's notice, never an instant eviction. Example: if you take a patrol bike and reach the station fight first, the capture and the report are your agency's; if the van down the hall gets there first, you can assist and share the credit for what you do. After any capture, the report goes into the Commission's incident app the same day, property damage needs photos and a witness, and the statement follows at the police Front Desk.

PEOPLE TO KNOW (the Row and the police, from their records):
- Kamui Woods and Gunhead: offices on the same hall. Kamui Woods is calm and courteous and competes for every call; Gunhead is soft-spoken and kind, and teaches the capture martial arts he fights with.
- Mount Lady and Fourth Kind: usually in the Ready Room. Mount Lady poses for any camera and needles rivals; Fourth Kind barks short orders and has no patience for excuses.
- Death Arms and Backdraft: usually in the Patrol Garage. Death Arms charges in first, shouting warnings; Backdraft works fires and rescues in crisp headcounts and instructions.
- Sansa Tamakawa: takes official statements at the Front Desk of Musutafu Police Headquarters; courteous and exact.
- Naomasa Tsukauchi: works major Quirk crimes from the Detectives' Office; calm, exact, and nobody lies to him twice.

WHAT THE PC CAN DO: take the call on foot or on a patrol bike, send your sidekick, radio the agency down the hall to coordinate, call the police, stay and settle the bills, press the first pin into the wall map, or knock on a neighbor's door. Every choice is yours.

RULES:
- Second person ("you"), present tense. The opening stays in the Agency Offices until you move.
- Your Quirk works exactly as your traits state; your license covers duty, and Commission paperwork follows every use.
- The agency starts small and grows only through play: one sidekick, one office manager, no famous clients.
- The Row's rivals are its canon pros: when the rival van needs a face, it belongs to one of the agencies named above, and that pro answers for it in person.
- Letting the call go is a real choice: the rival agency handles it, and the day moves on to the bills and the next call.
- Nothing of the coming year is promised or foreshadowed; outcomes stay wide open.
- End the opening on a live, open moment, not a question to the player.
Your Name on the Door.firstQuest: Make the agency real: win its first call on the Row, keep the sidekick paid, and put the agency's name on the map without a complaint on file.
Your Name on the Door.questGenerationGuidance: Favor the work of a small new agency: patrol calls, rival agencies, rent and payroll, sponsors, a first sidekick to lead, Commission paperwork and press attention. Canon events reach the agency as call-ups and news. Early quests stay small and paid: a patrol contract with a shopping street, a sponsor who wants a logo on the costume, an unpaid invoice, a complaint to answer, a team-up call from a bigger pro, the sidekick's first mistake. Stakes are money, the agency's good standing and the sidekick's trust; the agency's place on the Billboard Chart moves only through real work.
